extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, journalism educators, and students
extracted.subtask_description: Nine core principles from Kovach and Rosenstiel describing the ethical responsibilities, standards, and public-role obligations of journalists; presented as a teaching/resource packet with reflective essays and excerpts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism’s First Obligation Is to Tell the Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle One: the primary duty of journalism is to tell the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the foundational principle (Principle One). The issue pairs reflections and excerpts emphasizing truth-telling as journalism's first obligation; examples/articles in the issue discuss difficulties and demands of pursuing truth (e.g., "Making Truth an Idea That Journalists Can Believe in Again").

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism’s First Loyalty Is to Citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle Two: journalists' primary allegiance is to the public/citizens rather than to advertisers, owners, or other private interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeled as Principle Two. The collection frames loyalty to citizens as a central standard guiding editorial choices and newsroom priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Essence of Journalism Is a Discipline of Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle Three: journalism is fundamentally about verifying information through disciplined methods rather than mere assertion or advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked as Principle Three and excerpted from the book. Related articles emphasize verification practices (e.g., editors making writers pause to verify before publication) as an operational standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists Must Maintain an Independence From Those They Cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle Four: journalists should preserve independence from subjects of coverage to avoid conflicts of interest and preserve credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeled Principle Four. The issue includes essays on the challenges of retaining independence (e.g., pressure from owners, sources, or political forces) and on trade-offs when independence is compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists Must Serve as an Independent Monitor of Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are responsible for monitoring power and holding powerful actors accountable as a core public service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles discuss investigative reporting as recognition of this role (reference to the 1964 Pulitzer category for Investigative Reporting) and warn of consequences when the press fails to watchdog the powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism Must Provide a Forum for Public Criticism and Comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism should create and sustain public spaces where citizens can criticize, comment, and debate — enabling democratic conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue quotes that the forum function helps create democracy in large, diverse countries (invoking James Madison). Essays reflect on how newsrooms can facilitate serious public conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists Must Make the Significant Interesting and Relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should present important information in ways that engage audiences — bridging what people need to know with what will capture their attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue quotes: “This classic way of posing the question of engagement—as information versus storytelling, or what people need versus what people want—is a distortion. This is not how journalism is practiced,…" Emphasizes balancing storytelling and public importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists Should Keep the News in Proportion and Make It Comprehensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should provide proportionate, comprehensive coverage that helps citizens understand context and relative importance across issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as an editorial standard: 'Journalism is our modern cartography'—creating maps citizens use to navigate society. Encourages proportionality and comprehensiveness in coverage decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists Have an Obligation to Personal Conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must cultivate and act upon a personal sense of ethics and responsibility — a moral compass — and be willing to voice their conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue states: 'Every journalist—from the newsroom to the boardroom—must have a personal sense of ethics and responsibility—a moral compass.' Essays explore ethical decision-making and personal responsibility in newsroom contexts.
